questions.stem: Join the dots in order from \(1\) to \(5\) to form a polygon. In a, which shape is formed when all \(5\) dots are joined in order?

options: A pentagon with 5 straight sides and 5 corners
A quadrilateral with 4 straight sides and 4 corners
A hexagon with 6 straight sides and 6 corners
A triangle with 3 straight sides and 3 corners
questions.hint: Count how many numbered dots there are (\(1, 2, 3, 4, 5\)) and remember that "penta" means five, so a shape with \(5\) straight sides is a pentagon.

keyPoints.note: Joining 5 dots in a closed loop creates 5 straight sides and 5 corners, which is always a pentagon.

questions.solution: Joining dots \(1 \rightarrow 2 \rightarrow 3 \rightarrow 4 \rightarrow 5 \rightarrow 1\) forms a regular-looking convex pentagon with 5 straight sides and 5 corners.

options: A hexagon with 6 straight sides and 6 corners
A quadrilateral with 4 straight sides and 4 corners
A pentagon with 5 straight sides and 5 corners
An octagon with 8 straight sides and 8 corners
questions.hint: Count how many numbered dots there are (\(1, 2, 3, 4, 5\)) and remember that "penta" means five, so a shape with \(5\) straight sides is a pentagon.

keyPoints.note: Joining 5 dots in a closed loop creates 5 straight sides and 5 corners, which is always a pentagon.

questions.solution: Joining dots \(1 \rightarrow 2 \rightarrow 3 \rightarrow 4 \rightarrow 5 \rightarrow 1\) forms an irregular pentagon with 5 straight sides and 5 corners (with dot 4 pointing inward).

steps.explain: Locate the \(5\) numbered red dots and the given starting line between dot \(1\) and dot \(5\) (highlighted in orange).

questions.hint: A pentagon is any closed \(2\text{D}\) shape with exactly \(5\) straight sides and \(5\) corners (including both regular and irregular \(5\)-sided polygons).

keyPoints.text: which of the shapes are pentagons
keyPoints.note: Count the straight sides on every polygon—include both regular pentagons (5 equal sides) and irregular pentagons (any closed shape with 5 straight sides).

questions.solution: Shapes G and M are regular pentagons (\(5\) equal sides) and shapes K and L are irregular pentagons (\(5\) straight sides), so the pentagons are G, K, L, M.

steps.explain: Recall that "penta" means five: any closed polygon with \(5\) straight sides (regular or irregular) is a pentagon.

keyPoints.text: which of the shapes is a hexagon
keyPoints.note: Count the straight sides of each polygon and find the shape that has 6 straight sides.

questions.solution: Shape H has \(6\) straight sides and \(6\) corners, so H is a hexagon.

steps.explain: Recall that a hexagon is a closed \(2\text{D}\) shape with \(6\) straight sides and \(6\) corners.

options: Both shapes must be closed polygons with \(5\) straight sides and \(5\) corners.
Both shapes must have \(5\) equal sides and \(5\) equal angles.
Both shapes must be closed polygons with \(6\) straight sides and \(6\) corners.
Both shapes must have curved sides joining \(5\) dots.
questions.hint: Check the textbook definition at the top of the page: "Penta means five. A pentagon is a shape with five sides."

keyPoints.text: two different pentagons of your own
keyPoints.note: Any pentagon—regular or irregular—must be a closed shape with 5 straight sides and 5 corners.

questions.solution: Every pentagon (whether regular or irregular) is a closed polygon with \(5\) straight sides and \(5\) corners.

steps.explain: Review the definition of a pentagon: "penta" means five, so a pentagon is a closed shape with \(5\) straight sides and \(5\) corners (like example a highlighted in yellow).

No — the lines are not parallel because they cross or get closer together.
Yes — any two lines drawn inside the same box are parallel.

questions.hint: Check whether the lines in box a stay the exact same distance apart everywhere, or whether they cross / get closer together.

keyPoints.text: same distance apart are called parallel lines
keyPoints.note: Parallel lines do not have to be the same length and can point in any direction, as long as the distance between them never changes.

questions.solution: In box a, yes, the lines are parallel because the two horizontal straight lines are always the exact same distance apart and never meet.

keyPoints.text: same distance apart are called parallel lines
keyPoints.note: Parallel lines do not have to be the same length and can point in any direction, as long as the distance between them never changes.

questions.solution: In box b, yes, the lines are parallel because the two slanted straight lines are always the exact same distance apart (even though they have different lengths).

keyPoints.text: same distance apart are called parallel lines
keyPoints.note: Parallel lines do not have to be the same length and can point in any direction, as long as the distance between them never changes.

questions.solution: In box c, no, the lines are not parallel because the top slanted line gets closer to the bottom horizontal line and would meet it if extended.

keyPoints.text: same distance apart are called parallel lines
keyPoints.note: Parallel lines do not have to be the same length and can point in any direction, as long as the distance between them never changes.

Yes — any two lines drawn inside the same box are parallel.

questions.hint: Check whether the lines in box e stay the exact same distance apart everywhere, or whether they cross / get closer together.

keyPoints.text: same distance apart are called parallel lines
keyPoints.note: Parallel lines do not have to be the same length and can point in any direction, as long as the distance between them never changes.

questions.solution: In box e, no, the lines are not parallel because the two straight lines meet at a corner on the right.

questions.hint: Check whether the lines in box f stay the exact same distance apart everywhere, or whether they cross / get closer together.

keyPoints.text: same distance apart are called parallel lines
keyPoints.note: Parallel lines do not have to be the same length and can point in any direction, as long as the distance between them never changes.

questions.solution: In box f, no, the lines are not parallel because the horizontal line and vertical line cross (intersect) each other.

keyPoints.text: same distance apart are called parallel lines
keyPoints.note: Parallel lines do not have to be the same length and can point in any direction, as long as the distance between them never changes.

questions.solution: In box g, no, the lines are not parallel because the two straight lines cross each other in an X shape.

keyPoints.text: same distance apart are called parallel lines
keyPoints.note: Parallel lines do not have to be the same length and can point in any direction, as long as the distance between them never changes.

keyPoints.note: Parallel lines do not have to be the same length and can point in any direction, as long as the distance between them never changes.

questions.hint: Horizontal lines run across from left to right (like the horizon), whereas vertical lines run up and down.

keyPoints.note: Look for the straight lines on the table that go straight across from left to right.

questions.solution: The horizontal lines on the table are the long left-to-right edges of the tabletop and its apron rail.

steps.explain: Recall that a horizontal line runs straight across from left to right.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a set of parallel lines commonly found in a school classroom environment?
options: The opposite long edges of a whiteboard or classroom door
Two adjacent edges of a book that meet at a corner
The hands of the classroom clock at \(3\text{ o'clock}\)
The blades of an open pair of scissors meeting at the pivot
questions.hint: Look for two straight edges that never meet and stay the exact same distance apart.

keyPoints.text: parallel lines commonly found in a school classroom
keyPoints.note: Opposite edges of a rectangular whiteboard, desk, ruler, or door stay the same distance apart and never meet.

questions.solution: The opposite long edges of a rectangular whiteboard or classroom door stay the same distance apart everywhere and are parallel.

steps.explain: Recall that parallel lines are straight lines that stay the exact same distance apart and never meet.
Check the first option: the opposite edges of a rectangular whiteboard or door are always the same distance apart, so they are parallel.
Check the other options: adjacent book edges meet at a right-angle corner, clock hands at \(3\text{ o'clock}\) meet at the centre, and open scissor blades cross at the pivot.
Therefore, the opposite long edges of a whiteboard or classroom door are parallel lines.
steps.work: \(\text{Opposite edges of a whiteboard or door}\)

Rigid, because rectangles have 4 right angles that cannot change
Non-rigid, because it has only 3 sides

steps.explain: Recall the geometry rule for **rigidity**: a **triangle** is naturally **rigid** (its fixed side lengths lock its angles), whereas any polygon with \(4\) or more sides and no diagonal braces can hinge at its corners (**non-rigid**).

steps.explain: Recall the geometry rule for **rigidity**: a **triangle** is naturally **rigid** (its fixed side lengths lock its angles), whereas any polygon with \(4\) or more sides and no diagonal braces can hinge at its corners (**non-rigid**).

steps.explain: Recall the geometry rule for **rigidity**: a **triangle** is naturally **rigid** (its fixed side lengths lock its angles), whereas any polygon with \(4\) or more sides and no diagonal braces can hinge at its corners (**non-rigid**).

questions.hint: Triangles are rigid and keep their shape. Shapes with 4 or more sides are non-rigid unless they are divided into triangles by diagonal braces.

keyPoints.note: Check whether the frame is a triangle (or braced into triangles) or an unbraced polygon with 4+ sides.
Rigid means the shape cannot be squashed into a different shape when pushed.

questions.stem: Look at geostrip shape g (3-sided right-angled triangle frame). When you test this shape by gently pushing on its corners, is it rigid or non-rigid?

Non-rigid, because right-angled shapes always tilt into parallelograms
Rigid, because every 3-sided triangle frame is naturally rigid and holds its shape
Rigid, because it has a diagonal brace across the middle

steps.explain: Recall the geometry rule for **rigidity**: a **triangle** is naturally **rigid** (its fixed side lengths lock its angles), whereas any polygon with \(4\) or more sides and no diagonal braces can hinge at its corners (**non-rigid**).

keyPoints.note: Check whether the frame is a triangle (or braced into triangles) or an unbraced polygon with 4+ sides.
Rigid means the shape cannot be squashed into a different shape when pushed.

questions.stem: Compare geostrip shape a (an unbraced square) and geostrip shape h (a square with a diagonal geostrip). Why was shape h rigid while shape a was non-rigid?

options: 2 geostrips, because two diagonals from one corner divide the pentagon into 3 rigid triangles
1 geostrip, because one diagonal divides the pentagon into 2 rigid triangles
5 geostrips, because every corner needs its own extra geostrip to be rigid
0 geostrips, because a 5-sided pentagon is already rigid on its own

steps.explain: If we add just **1 diagonal** geostrip connecting two corners of the pentagon, it splits the pentagon into \(1\) triangle and \(1\) quadrilateral (4-sided shape), which can still flex.

keyPoints.note: When you fold a shape along a line of symmetry, the two halves match completely.

questions.solution: Shape f (blue equilateral triangle (all three sides equal)) has \(3\) lines of symmetry.

questions.stem: When you fold a 2D shape along any of its lines of symmetry, does each line of symmetry break the shape into two identical matching halves?

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 280 175" width="65%" height="auto" style="max-width:351px;display:block;margin:0 auto;"><rect x="4" y="4" width="272" height="167" rx="10" fill="#f8fafc" stroke="#cbd5e1" stroke-width="2"/><rect x="94" y="34" width="92" height="92" fill="#fde047" fill-opacity="0.85" stroke="#0f172a" stroke-width="2.2"/></svg>

options: Yes, because a line of symmetry divides a shape into two identical mirror-image halves that fit on top of each other exactly
No, because one half is always larger than the other half when folded
No, because only circles can be divided into two identical halves
Yes, because any straight line drawn across a shape is always a line of symmetry

steps.explain: Draw the lines of symmetry on a 2D shape (such as the vertical, horizontal, and diagonal lines of symmetry on a square).

steps.explain: By definition, when you fold a shape along a **line of symmetry**, the two halves match up edge-for-edge and corner-for-corner with no overlap left over.

questions.hint: Multiply the number of rows by the number of columns for each rectangle and find the pair where both products equal 12.

keyPoints.text: different shapes that cover the same area
keyPoints.note: Two different rectangles have the same area if rows × columns gives the same number of squares.

questions.solution: A \(3 \times 4\) rectangle covers \(12\) squares and a \(2 \times 6\) rectangle also covers \(12\) squares.

steps.explain: To find the area of a rectangle on grid paper, multiply the number of rows by the number of columns.

questions.stem: Use Base 10 flats, exercise books or envelopes to measure the area of your desk. Since a Base 10 flat is smaller than an exercise book, how will the number of Base 10 flats needed to cover the desk compare to the number of exercise books?

options: More Base 10 flats than exercise books are needed because each flat has a smaller area.
Fewer Base 10 flats than exercise books are needed because each flat has a smaller area.
The exact same number of Base 10 flats and exercise books are needed to cover the desk.
Fewer Base 10 flats than exercise books are needed because each book has a smaller area.
questions.hint: Think about covering the same desk: does a smaller tile take more pieces or fewer pieces to cover the same surface?

keyPoints.text: Base 10 flats, exercise books or envelopes to measure the area of your desk
keyPoints.note: Smaller measuring units require a larger number of units to cover the same area.

questions.solution: Because a Base 10 flat has a smaller area than an exercise book, it takes more Base 10 flats than exercise books to cover the same desk.

steps.explain: Compare the size of the two units: a Base 10 flat (\(10\text{ cm} \times 10\text{ cm}\)) is much smaller than an exercise book.
steps.work: \(\text{Area of Base 10 flat} < \text{Area of exercise book}\)

options: Rectangular units fit together edge-to-edge without leaving gaps or overlaps.
Rectangular units leave large circular gaps between them that are easy to count.
Different-sized rectangular units can be mixed together in the same area count.
Overlapping the rectangular units on top of each other gives the exact area.
questions.hint: Look at how the rectangular books/flats sit next to one another on the desk top.

keyPoints.text: most suitable for measuring the desk
keyPoints.note: Good area units must be uniform in size and tile (fit together) without gaps or overlaps.

questions.solution: Rectangular units (such as exercise books, envelopes, or Base 10 flats) are suitable because their straight edges fit together edge-to-edge with no gaps and no overlaps.

steps.explain: Look at the rectangular units arranged across the rectangular desk surface.

questions.stem: Jacqui covered her desk with round ice-cream lids. Do you think these are good measuring units for area, and why?

options: Yes, because circular lids are much easier to trace around than square tiles.
No, because round lids cannot fit together without leaving gaps between them.
Yes, because the uncovered gaps between the round lids do not have any area.
No, because round lids are too heavy to place flat on top of a student desk.
questions.hint: Look closely at the spaces between the round ice-cream lids on Jacqui’s desk.

keyPoints.note: Circles have curved edges, so placing them side by side always leaves uncovered spaces (gaps) in between.

questions.solution: No, round ice-cream lids are not good measuring units for area because curved circles leave uncovered gaps between them.

meta.question: 10h

questions.stem: The base of a Base 10 flat is a \(10\text{ cm} \times 10\text{ cm}\) square with an area of \(100\text{ cm}^2\). In a, which option gives surface(s) with an area smaller than \(100\text{ cm}^2\)?
options: An eraser and a postage stamp
A classroom door and a student desk top
A whiteboard and a classroom floor rug
An A4 exercise book cover and a classroom window
questions.hint: Picture a \(10\text{ cm}\) by \(10\text{ cm}\) Base 10 flat (about the size of your palm) and compare each object's surface to it.

keyPoints.note: One Base 10 flat has 10 rows of 10 square centimetres = 100 cm².

questions.solution: An eraser and a postage stamp are much smaller than a \(10\text{ cm} \times 10\text{ cm}\) Base 10 flat, so their areas are smaller than \(100\text{ cm}^2\).

steps.explain: Understand the benchmark area: the base of one Base 10 flat is \(10\text{ cm}\) wide and \(10\text{ cm}\) long, so its area is \(10 \times 10 = 100\text{ cm}^2\).
An eraser and a postage stamp are much smaller than a \(10\text{ cm} \times 10\text{ cm}\) Base 10 flat, so their areas are smaller than \(100\text{ cm}^2\).
Check the other choices to confirm they do not match the condition "area smaller than \(100\text{ cm}^2\)".
Therefore, the correct choice is: An eraser and a postage stamp.

meta.question: 11b

questions.stem: The base of a Base 10 flat is a \(10\text{ cm} \times 10\text{ cm}\) square with an area of \(100\text{ cm}^2\). In c, which option gives surface(s) with an area about \(100\text{ cm}^2\)?
options: A classroom door measuring \(200\text{ cm}\) by \(80\text{ cm}\)
A pencil sharpener measuring \(3\text{ cm}\) by \(2\text{ cm}\)
A square sticky note or coaster measuring \(10\text{ cm}\) by \(10\text{ cm}\)
A tiny postage stamp measuring \(2\text{ cm}\) by \(2\text{ cm}\)
questions.hint: Picture a \(10\text{ cm}\) by \(10\text{ cm}\) Base 10 flat (about the size of your palm) and compare each object's surface to it.

keyPoints.note: One Base 10 flat has 10 rows of 10 square centimetres = 100 cm².

questions.solution: A square coaster or sticky note measuring \(10\text{ cm}\) by \(10\text{ cm}\) has the same area as one Base 10 flat (\(10 \times 10 = 100\text{ cm}^2\)).

steps.explain: Understand the benchmark area: the base of one Base 10 flat is \(10\text{ cm}\) wide and \(10\text{ cm}\) long, so its area is \(10 \times 10 = 100\text{ cm}^2\).
A square coaster or sticky note measuring \(10\text{ cm}\) by \(10\text{ cm}\) has the same area as one Base 10 flat (\(10 \times 10 = 100\text{ cm}^2\)).
Check the other choices to confirm they do not match the condition "area about \(100\text{ cm}^2\)".
Therefore, the correct choice is: A square sticky note or coaster measuring \(10\text{ cm}\) by \(10\text{ cm}\).
